title: When AI designs a drug, who gets the credit?
gist: US patent law requires a human 'inventor,' so AI drug-discovery companies like Insilico Medicine publicly credit their AI for finding a molecule but list only humans on the actual patent -- a workaround that patent attorney Ryan Abbott warns could later be challenged, especially now that the Trump-era USPTO treats AI as a mere tool requiring no disclosure at all.

insights.claim: Insilico Medicine publicly credited its generative AI platform with 'discovering' a drug candidate for pulmonary fibrosis, but when filing the actual patent to protect the chemical structure, the company listed no AI and instead named five humans, including CEO Alex Zhavoronkov, as the inventors.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: A clear real-world example of the gap between AI-drug marketing claims and the legal paperwork -- useful for evaluating how literally to take any AI biotech's 'AI-discovered' claims.
insights.quote: the patent names five humans, including CEO Alex Zhavoronkov, as the drug’s “inventors.”

insights.claim: Insilico's CEO says human chemists still synthesize candidate molecules, create variants, and test them on animals, and that even in a hypothetical fully-roboticized future pipeline, whoever 'pushes the button and gives the budget' would still be the named patent inventor -- indicating AI drug companies are deliberately keeping documented humans in the loop to preserve patentability.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Signals that AI drug-discovery firms are structuring their R&D workflows around current patent law's human-inventor requirement, a compliance cost that could shift if the law changes.

insights.claim: In 2022, a DC appeals court ruled in the DABUS test case that an AI cannot be named a patent inventor, because US statute defines 'inventor' as an 'individual,' whose plain meaning is a human being -- regardless of any 'metaphysical' questions about AI's role in a discovery.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Establishes the binding US legal precedent (human-only inventorship) that every AI drug/invention company currently must structure its patent filings around.
insights.quote: US statutes describe an inventor as an “individual,” the plain meaning of which is a human being.
insights.locator: The case might have raised philosophical questions

insights.claim: Regulators and legal experts now concede that AI systems can perform acts that would count as 'inventorship' if a human did them; the live open question is no longer whether AI can invent but whether any human involved contributed enough to legitimately be named an inventor.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Reframes the real legal battleground for AI-invention companies: proving sufficient human contribution on each patent, not debating AI personhood.
insights.quote: an AI system—like other tools—may perform acts that, if performed by a human, could constitute inventorship under our laws
insights.locator: That’s partly because no one is denying that AIs can invent

insights.claim: Sarah Korman, chief business and legal officer at Isomorphic Labs, states there must be a human inventor for a patent to exist at all under current law, while acknowledging that patent law will 'no doubt' need to evolve to keep pace with AI-driven discovery.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: A senior legal officer at a major AI-drug-discovery spinout (Isomorphic Labs) publicly confirming the human-inventor requirement signals how the industry is currently operating within, not against, existing law.
insights.quote: There needs to be a human inventor or there’s no invention and no patent

insights.claim: US patent-office policy on AI inventorship reversed after the change in administration: the Biden-era USPTO published guidance to help applicants determine when humans truly qualify as AI co-inventors, but the current office now treats AI as merely a tool 'like a calculator' that requires no mention at all.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: A material, administration-driven swing in patent-office guidance changes how much disclosure AI-drug and AI-invention companies now need to provide -- worth tracking as a compliance and political risk.
insights.quote: Now the patent office says AI is merely a tool, like a calculator. No need to even mention it.

insights.claim: The US Copyright Office is separately refusing to grant copyrights to AI-generated images and text, a stance drawing pushback from content-industry groups such as the Motion Picture Association of America.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Shows the human-authorship requirement is being applied consistently across IP regimes (patents and copyright), not just in biotech, which broadens the relevance to any AI-content or AI-generative business.

insights.claim: Patent attorney Ryan Abbott warns AI-generated drug patents face a latent invalidation risk: one way to strike down a patent is to show it lists the wrong inventors, so if a listed human's contribution is later found insufficient, the patent -- and the drug's protection -- could be challenged, potentially chilling AI-driven drug development.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: A real legal tail risk for AI-drug-discovery companies' patent portfolios: mislisted inventorship is grounds for invalidation, which could undercut the value of AI-discovered drug IP.
insights.quote: Abbott believes there could be legal challenges to AI-generated drugs, since one way to invalidate a patent is to show it has the wrong inventors listed.

insights.claim: Abbott poses an open legal test case -- asking Claude to 'cure cancer' and having it succeed -- arguing it would be inappropriate for the human prompter alone to claim inventorship, underscoring how far current law lags behind highly autonomous AI-driven discovery.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Highlights the coming attribution problem as AI systems become more autonomous in generating discoveries with minimal human direction, a scenario current patent doctrine doesn't cleanly resolve.
insights.quote: What if I asked Claude to cure cancer, and it did?
